docs.title: Build a Dart API with Dox
docs.text:
This post shows how to go from an empty folder to a tested API with a database, validation and a native binary, in a few short steps.

Each step has a small code block and a link to its docs page. The code comes from the tutorial, which builds a small blog API.

docs.title: 1. Install the CLI and make a project
docs.text:
You need Dart 3.13 or newer.

dart pub global activate dox
dox create blog
cd blog
dart pub get

dox create downloads the starter project and makes a .env file with a new random APP_KEY. The starter project uses SQLite, so there is no database to install.

Docs: Installation

docs.title: 2. Start the server
docs.text:
dox s

dox s is short for dox serve. It runs the code generator and the server. It restarts the server when you save a .dart file.

curl http://localhost:3000/api/ping

pong

Docs: Step 1: Create the project

docs.title: 3. Make a model and a migration
docs.text:
Stop dox s first with Ctrl+C. dox s restarts the server when a new file appears, and the server runs new migrations at start. So it would run the new migration before you add the columns.

One command makes the model and the migration:

dox make:model Post -m

Add the columns to the migration:

db/migration/<date>_create_posts_table.dart
await schema.create('posts', (Table table) {
  table.id();
  table.string('title');
  table.text('body');
  table.timestamps();
});

Add the same fields to the model:

lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart
@DoxModel(table: 'posts')
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? title;

  @Column()
  String? body;
}

Then run the migration:

dox migration:run

Then start dox s again. The server also runs new migrations each time it starts.

Docs: Step 2: Model and migration, Model

docs.title: 4. Add a controller and routes
docs.text:
dox make:controller Post -r

A controller method can return a model or a list of models. Dox sends it as JSON.

lib/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart
@Inject()
class PostController {
  Future<List<Post>> index(DoxRequest req) async {
    return Post().all();
  }

  Future<Post> show(int id) async {
    Post? post = await Post().find(id);
    if (post == null) {
      throw NotFoundHttpException();
    }
    return post;
  }
}

One line adds the routes:

lib/routes/api.dart
Route.resource('posts', PostController);

Route.resource makes a route for each method the controller has. Here that is GET /api/posts and GET /api/posts/{id}. Dox makes the controller for you, because it has @Inject().

Docs: Step 3: Routes and controller, Routing

docs.title: 5. Check the input with a DTO
docs.text:
dox make:dto SavePost

A DTO is a class with rules on its fields:

lib/app/dtos/save_post/save_post.dto.dart
@Dto()
class SavePost {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 3, max: 100)
  final String title;

  @Trim()
  @MinLength(10)
  final String body;

  const SavePost({required this.title, required this.body});

  static const DtoSchema<SavePost> schema = $SavePostDto;
}

Ask for it as a parameter in the controller:

Future<DoxResponse> store(SavePost body) async {
  Post post = Post()
    ..title = body.title
    ..body = body.body;
  await post.save();
  return response(post).statusCode(201);
}

Dox checks the body before the method runs. Your code gets a typed object. Bad input gets a 422 answer with one message for each field:

{"title":"The title must be between 3 and 100 characters","body":"The body must be at least 10 characters"}

Add two lines to lib/config/app.dart, so the app knows the DTOs:

lib/config/app.dart
import 'package:blog/generated/dtos.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  dtos: dtos,
  // ... the rest stays the same
);

Docs: Step 4: Validation, Validation

docs.title: 6. Write a test
docs.text:
DoxTestClient starts the app inside the test, on a free port.

test/http_test.dart
void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
  });

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('GET /api/posts gives a list', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.get('/api/posts');
    res.expectStatus(200).expectJson(isA<List<dynamic>>());
  });
}

dart test

The full test in the tutorial also runs the migrations first, so it works on an empty database.

Docs: Step 6: Test, Testing

docs.title: 7. Build one binary
docs.text:
dox build

dox build runs the code generator, then compiles the app. The result is in build/bundle. bin/server is one native binary. It does not need the Dart SDK.

cd build/bundle
cp ../../.env .env
./bin/server

The project also has a Dockerfile that builds the same bundle into a small image.

Docs: Step 7: Build and deploy, Docker

docs.title: What you have now
docs.text:
• A server that restarts when you save a file.
  • A database table, a model and a migration.
  • Routes and a controller that return JSON.
  • Input checks with a typed DTO and a 422 answer for bad input.
  • A test that runs the real app.
  • One binary for production.

The tutorial does all of this in full, and adds login with dox_auth in step 5.

docs.title: Dox 3.1 is out
docs.text:
Dox 3.1 adds new routing tools, request helpers, new ORM features, access tokens, a new MCP package, mail and queue features, and many security and bug fixes.

This post covers 3.1.0 (November 8) and the two patch releases after it, 3.1.1 and 3.1.2 (November 9). A change that came in a patch has its version after it, like "(3.1.1)". Everything else came in 3.1.0.

docs.title: How to update
docs.text:
1. Update the dox CLI:

    dox update

  2. In your pubspec.yaml, set the Dox packages to ^3.1.0 (or newer), then get them:

    dart pub upgrade

  3. Make the generated code again. Relations and DTOs get new code in 3.1.

    dox build_runner:build

  4. Read the next section. Some changes need a code change.

docs.title: Read before you update
docs.text: These changes can change how your app works.

docs.title: ORM
docs.text:
• Models are guarded by default. guarded is now ['*']. A model with no fillable list throws MassAssignmentException when create(), update(), insert(), upsert(), firstOrCreate() or a similar method gets a map. Before, it took every key, so User().create(req.body) could set id or is_admin. To fix it, add fillable with the columns a map may set. Or set guarded to const <String>[] to take every key, as before. save() and fields you set in code do not change. See Mass assignment.
  • A write with no key and no where() throws. Blog().delete(), Blog().update({...}), forceDelete(), increment() and decrement() on a model with no primary key value and no where() used to change every row of the table. Now they throw a StateError and run no query. To change every row on purpose, use Blog().whereRaw('1 = 1').delete() (or .update()). restore() on a query with no where() throws too.
  • findOrFail() and firstOrFail() answer 404, not 500. ModelNotFoundException is now an HTTP exception with code 404. Its constructor is no longer const.
  • A digit in a model name gets no _. Address2 now gives the table address2, the foreign key address2_id, the pivot table address2_tag and the count key address2_count. Before, it was address_2. If you use these default names, rename the table or column, or set tableName, foreignKey and the pivot names by hand.
  • New many to many methods on every model: attach, detach, sync, syncWithoutDetaching, toggle, updateExistingPivot and pivot. A @Scope() with one of these names is hidden when you call it right on a model, like Song().sync(). Rename such a scope.
  • A nullable list relation is [] after a preload with no rows, not null. For example List<Tag>? tags. Run build_runner again.
  • @Unique trusts the database. On MySQL and MariaDB, text compares without case. So TAKEN@dox.dev now fails @Unique when taken@dox.dev is in the table.
  • update() and delete() with groupBy() or having() throw an ArgumentError. The SQL was never valid.

docs.title: Routing and core
docs.text:
• RateLimit counts are shared by all isolates (without Redis). max now holds for the whole server, not for each isolate. An app with more than one isolate gets a lower real limit than before. Raise max if you need the old number.
  • Route.mount matches whole path parts. A mount at /admin gets /admin and /admin/..., but no longer /administrator. When two mount prefixes match, the longest one wins. Before, the first one added won.
  • Removed helpers: getDoxRequest and middlewareAndControllerHandler are gone from dox_core. They were not used. Use DoxRequest.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
• IpRule is no longer a RegexRule, so IpRule().pattern is gone.
  • v.string().ip() now takes IPv6 too, like @Ip. Its JSON Schema is anyOf IPv4 and IPv6.
  • ip() and @Ip now say no to IPv4 addresses with leading zeros, like 01.1.1.1.
  • alphaDash() and @AlphaDash now allow digits, like post-123. The message and the JSON Schema pattern change too.
  • email() now takes + and ' before the @, like ann+tag@x.com.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
• dox exits with code 1 when there is no command, an unknown command, bad arguments, or a command that throws. Before, it exited with 0.
  • dox make:model Post now writes @DoxModel(table: 'posts'), the same plural table that -m makes. The new model has an empty fillable list.
  • migration:fresh, migration:reset, migration:refresh, migration:rollback and key:generate ask first when APP_ENV=production and you run them in a terminal. --force skips the question. Without a terminal (CI, deploy scripts), they print a warning and run as before.
  • dox make:serializer makes the file in lib/app/serializers/, not lib/app/http/serializers/ (3.1.1).

docs.title: Other packages
docs.text:
• Queue: deploy the queue worker together with the web app. An old worker does not know the new built-in mail job, so it fails queued emails. dox_queue now depends on dox_mailer.
  • Custom queue drivers: release() must now also save job.payload, so the worker can keep the exception count. The new clear() and pruneFailed() throw an UnsupportedError on a custom driver that does not override them.
  • Storage: url() on a local disk with no url option gives /storage/<path>. Before, it threw. New signed URLs include the disk name, so they do not work on 3.0.1. During a rolling deploy, they can get 403 until they expire. A signed Storage.route() on a disk that is not local still gives 403, and now also reports an UnsupportedOperationException.
  • Mail: Attachment.fromFile reads the file when the message is sent or queued, so a missing file now throws from send().
  • Views: components always get $slot and $slots.main, as empty text when there is no body. So {{ $slots.main ?? 'x' }} no longer prints x. An empty SafeString is false in @if.
  • OpenAPI: a route with an optional param, like /greet/{name?}, gives two paths: /greet/{name} and /greet. The short path gets its own summary and operation id.
  • Inertia: an empty 200 answer to an Inertia request now goes back to the page it came from.

docs.title: Routing
docs.text:
• Route.match(methods, path, handler) and Route.any(path, handler).
  • Route.redirect(from, to) (302) and Route.permanentRedirect(from, to) (301).
  • .where(param, regex): the route matches only when the param matches the regex. The value is checked after % decoding, and a leading ^ and trailing $ are fine.
  • Route.fallback(handler) answers a GET or HEAD that matches no route. It follows the group prefix, also one with a param like {tenant}.
  • Route.staticFiles(prefix, folder, maxAge:) serves a folder, with ETag, Last-Modified, 304 and Range support. Files in .well-known are served too. The folders reach every isolate.
  • MethodOverride middleware: a plain HTML form can reach Route.put, Route.patch and Route.delete with a _method field. MethodOverride(header: true) also reads the X-HTTP-Method-Override header.
  • Route.mount(prefix, handler, middleware: true) runs the global middleware before a raw handler.
  • Route.websocket(maxMessageSize:).
  • AppConfig.idleTimeout and AppConfig.maxConnections for the server.
  • In development, a warning when a middleware returns null.
Route.redirect('/home', '/');
Route.get('/users/{id}', (UserController c) => c.show).where('id', '[0-9]+');
Route.staticFiles('/', 'public');
Route.fallback((DoxRequest req) {
  return response(<String, String>{'message': 'Page not found'}).statusCode(404);
});

Docs: Routing, Static files, Native server

docs.title: Requests and responses
docs.text:
• req.input(key, defaultValue) with dot keys, like user.name or items.0.id.
  • filled, exists, missing, except, boolean and integer.
  • file(key) and hasFile(key) for uploads.
  • bearerToken(), path(), fullUrl(), pathIs(pattern) and routeIs(pattern). pathIs() cleans the path like the router, so /admin/ and /admin// match admin.
  • req.auth?.id() gives the id of the logged-in user.
  • SessionMiddleware().fromCookie(value) loads a session with no request, for a Socket.IO login.
  • DoxCookie.decrypt(name, value) decrypts a cookie value.
  • RequestBody and BodyKind are exported, so req.requestBody.kind can tell invalid JSON from no body (3.1.1).
  • ValidationException.issues keeps every issue of a failed check, for your own 422 shape (3.1.1).
  • RequestFile.head keeps more bytes of an upload, so image size checks work.

Docs: Request, Session

docs.title: Security, encryption and cache
docs.text:
• WebSocket Origin check: Route.websocket(allowedOrigins: [...]) or AppConfig.webSocketAllowedOrigins. It is off by default. A WebSocket route with no check prints a warning at start.
  • A warning when CORS has origin * together with credentials: true.
  • Crypt.encryptString, Crypt.decryptString, Crypt.encrypt and Crypt.decrypt with the APP_KEY. A value that can not be decrypted throws DecryptException (400).
  • Hash.check, the same as Hash.verify.
  • Hash.sha256(value) to store API keys and tokens as a hash (3.1.1). Do not use it for passwords.
  • Cache().many(keys) and Cache().putMany(values).
  • Cache().flexible takes a null stale: it keeps the last good value until a refresh replaces it (3.1.1).
  • The file cache driver can delete old files by itself, with the prune_every option.

Docs: Encryption, Hashing, Cache

docs.title: Validation and DTOs
docs.text:
• New rules, each as a fluent rule and a DTO annotation: same / @Same, confirmed / @Confirmed, requiredIf / @RequiredIf, requiredWith / @RequiredWith, json / @Json, digits / @Digits, digitsBetween / @DigitsBetween, dateFormat / @DateFormatted and password / @Password.
  • between(1, 10) on v.int() and v.num().
  • exists('teams') and unique('users', column: 'email') in fluent schemas. The ORM answers them.
  • File rules: maxSize, minSize / @MinSize, mimes, mimeTypes / @MimeTypes and dimensions / @Dimensions. The MIME type is checked against the real file bytes.
  • hexColor() / @HexColor() (3.1.1).
  • @Dto(emptyStringsToNull: true) reads "" as null (3.1.1).
  • @OrDefault() gives a field its default for a bad value, not an error. Use it for query strings like ?page=abc (3.1.1).
  • @Describe('...') puts a description in the JSON Schema of a field and in the OpenAPI docs (3.1.2).
  • @Dto(messages:) matches the full dotted path first, like tags.*.required.
  • RuleContext.sibling('key') reads another key of the same object.
  • ImageSize.read(head), FileTypes.matchesMimeTypes and FileTypes.extensionsOf for your own file rules.
  • The build stops with a clear error when a rule names a Dart field instead of its input key.
@Dto()
class Register {
  @Describe('Shown on the profile page.')
  @Length(min: 1, max: 40)
  final String name;

  @Password(min: 8, mixedCase: true, numbers: true)
  @Confirmed()
  final String password;

  @RequiredIf('type', 'company')
  final String? vat;

  // ...
}

Docs: Validation, Validation rules

docs.title: ORM and database
docs.text:
• Many to many writes: attach(), detach(), sync(), syncWithoutDetaching(), toggle() and updateExistingPivot().
  • @ManyToMany(withPivot: [...], withTimestamps: true) reads extra pivot columns, with song.pivot['role'].
  • Polymorphic relations: @MorphMany, @MorphOne and @MorphTo, with Model.morphMap().
  • Pages: simplePaginate() (no total count) and cursorPaginate() (a page after a cursor, no OFFSET).
  • Sub queries: whereIn() with a query or any Iterable (like a Set), joinSub(), leftJoinSub() and fromSub().
  • union() and unionAll(). Read a union with get(). Methods that need one row or one part, like find() or pluck(), throw a StateError on a union.
  • Dates: whereDate(), whereTime(), whereYear(), whereMonth() and whereDay().
  • JSON: whereJsonContains() and whereJsonDoesntContain().
  • whereNot(column, value), orWhereNot(), unless() and whenValue().
  • first() and doesntExist(), the same as getFirst() and hasNoRows().
  • insertGetId(), insertMany() and insertOrIgnore().
  • onlyTrashed(), touch(), touchQuietly() and replicate().
  • withAvg(), withMin() and withExists().
  • forceCreate(), forceUpdate(), forceFill() and Model.unguarded() skip fillable and guarded. Do not pass user input to them. forceFill() throws an ArgumentError when it can not set a column.
  • toRawSql() gives the SQL with the values in it, for logs.
  • ConnectionConfig.logRedact hides values, like passwords, in the query log. Each named connection uses its own list.
  • FileQueryPrinter(buffered: true) writes the query log in the background.
  • Schema helpers: foreignIdFor(), ulid(), foreignUlid(), year(), ipAddress(), softDeletesTz(), nullableMorphs(), uuidMorphs(), dropTimestamps(), dropSoftDeletes(), dropConstrainedForeignId(), dropPrimary(), renameIndex(), fullText(), nullOnUpdate() and restrictOnUpdate().
  • Postgres with useSSL: true prints a warning that the server certificate is not checked. Set extra['sslMode'] = 'verify-full' to check it.
  • MySQL: the new sslRootCert option (URL option ssl_ca) trusts a private CA. Without TLS, it prints a warning that it is ignored.
  • MySQL: a pool that can not open now says why.
  • find(5, null) throws a clear ArgumentError: the first arg must be a column name.
  • package:dox_migration/env.dart exports loadEnv.
// many to many
PivotSyncResult result = await artist.sync('songs', <int>[1, 2, 3]);

// a page after a cursor
CursorPagination<Blog> page = await Blog()
    .orderBy('id')
    .cursorPaginate(perPage: 10, cursor: req.input('cursor'));

Docs: Query builder, Model, Many to many, Polymorphic, Schema, Pagination

docs.title: Auth
docs.text:
• Access tokens, opt-in. A token looks like oat_<id>.<secret>. The table keeps only a hash of the secret. Each token has a name, abilities and an expiry.
  • dox auth:tokens-table writes the migration for the access tokens table.
  • AuthMiddleware(guards: ['web', 'api']) tries several guards in order.
  • AuthMiddleware(optional: true) lets guests through too, so req.can() works on a public page.
  • GuestMiddleware lets only guests through, for login and register pages.
  • Auth().check(), Auth().id(), Auth().guest() and Auth().once(credentials).
  • Auth().userFromToken(token) and Auth().userFromSession(session) check a login with no request, like in Socket.IO.
  • Opt-in login throttle: Auth.throttle = LoginThrottle(...). Give the ip with Auth(ip: req.ip()).
  • Opt-in JWT revocation: JwtAuthDriver(revocation: true), with revokeToken, revokeAllTokens and forgetUser.
  • Opt-in small JWT: JwtAuthDriver(minimalPayload: true) puts only the user id in the token.
  • Auth.needsRehash(hash) and Auth.hashCost(hash) to raise the password hash cost.
  • JwtAuthDriver.bearerToken(req) reads the token. AuthDriver.reportError() reports errors.
  • New JWTs carry a jti claim. Tokens made before still work.
  • The error of logout() on a token guard now says to use revokeToken().

No auth change is breaking. Apps work the same with no code change, and no user is logged out.

AccessToken token = await Auth(guard: 'api').createAccessToken(
  user,
  name: 'cli',
  abilities: <String>['posts:read'],
  expiresIn: const Duration(days: 30),
);
return <String, dynamic>{'token': token.value}; // shown only once

Docs: Authentication

docs.title: MCP
docs.text:
dox_mcp is a new package. It turns a Dox app into an MCP server, so AI tools can call your code.

  • McpServer (Streamable HTTP), McpTool with dox_validation input schemas, McpTool.of, McpToolResult and McpContext.
  • SignedMcpSessions: session ids signed with the APP_KEY.
  • McpOAuth: the OAuth 2.1 sign-in of the MCP spec, with PKCE and dynamic client registration (3.1.1). From 3.1.2, the code_verifier, code_challenge and redirect address are checked strictly.
  • McpDtoTool<T>: a tool that takes a @Dto class as its input. handle gets the typed object. McpToolResult.invalidArguments() gives the error result for bad arguments (3.1.2).
class CreateCategory extends McpDtoTool<NewCategory> {
  @override
  String get name => 'create_category';

  @override
  String get description => 'Add a category.';

  @override
  DtoSchema<NewCategory> get dto => NewCategory.schema;

  @override
  Future<McpToolResult> handle(NewCategory input, McpContext context) async {
    return McpToolResult.text('Added ${input.name}.');
  }
}

Docs: MCP

docs.title: Queue
docs.text:
• Queue.fake() for tests, with assertPushed, assertPushedTimes, assertNotPushed and assertNothingPushed.
  • Job settings: retryUntil, maxExceptions and failOnTimeout.
  • dispatch(delayUntil: DateTime), dispatchIf() and dispatchUnless().
  • Worker flags: --backoff, --max-jobs, --max-time, --memory and --timeout-grace.
  • Commands: dox queue:clear, dox queue:restart, dox queue:prune-failed and dox queue:table.
  • ShouldBeEncrypted: save the job data encrypted with the APP_KEY.
  • A built-in job sends Mail.queue() and Mail.later().
  • QueueConfig.redisFromEnv() reads the Redis server from REDIS_URL, or from REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT, REDIS_USERNAME, REDIS_PASSWORD and REDIS_TLS.

Docs: Queue

docs.title: Mail and notifications
docs.text:
• Mailables: one class per kind of email, with send(), queue() and later().
  • Markdown mail, from a dox_view template. A text value from data stays text. Pass a SafeString to put Markdown from a value.
  • MailMessage: an email made of lines and a button, with no template.
  • Notifications: Notification, MailChannel, Notifiable and your own channels.
  • Mail.queue() and Mail.later() send the email from the job queue. With encrypt: true, a send error in the log does not show the recipient.
  • Message.toJson() and Message.fromJson(), and the MailQueue interface with Mail.useQueue().
  • Mail.raw(), and Mail.to(...).cc(...).bcc(...).send(...).
  • Mail.alwaysTo(address) sends every email to one address, for example on staging.
  • Mail.onSending() and Mail.onSent() hooks, and Mail.clearHooks().
  • Test checks on Mail.fake(): assertSent, assertSentCount, assertNotSent, assertNothingSent, assertQueued, assertNotQueued and assertNothingQueued.

Docs: Mail, Notifications

docs.title: Scheduler
docs.text:
• ScheduleConfig(timezone: ...): the default time zone of every task.
  • environments(['production']): run a task only in these environments.
  • unlessBetween(start, end).
  • New frequencies, like everyTwoHours, twiceDailyAt, lastDayOfMonth, quarterly, yearlyOn and mondays() to sundays().
  • A warning when onOneServer() uses a lock store that is not shared between servers.
  • Scheduler.close() frees the overlap locks.
  • When a provider's setup() throws, SchedulerRunner shuts down the providers that already started.

Docs: Scheduler

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
• append(), prepend(), size(), lastModified(), makeDirectory() and directoryExists().
  • temporaryUrl(), the same as signedUrl().
  • file.store(folder, disk: 's3'), file.storeAs(folder, name) and Storage().putRequestFileAs().
  • atomic_writes: a failed upload never leaves a half-written file.
  • assertExists() and assertMissing() on a fake disk, for tests.

Docs: File storage

docs.title: Socket.IO
docs.text:
• SocketAuth logs a socket in at connect time. The user is in socket.user.
  • handshake.token, handshake.cookie(name) and await handshake.session().
  • ServerOptions(allowedOrigins:) turns on an origin check.

Docs: Socket.IO

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
• New tags: @isset, @empty, @auth, @guest, @env, @production, @once, @verbatim, @class, @checked, @selected and @disabled.
  • Components get $attributes (with merge()) and $slot.
  • ViewEngine(environment:) sets the environment for @env and @production. By default it is APP_ENV.

Docs: Views

docs.title: Inertia
docs.text:
• Inertia.render(), the same as inertia(), and Inertia.lazy, the same as Inertia.optional.
  • Inertia.shareGlobal(key, value) shares a prop with every page.
  • A deferred prop can be merged: Inertia.defer(fn).merge().
  • The asset version is checked before the controller runs, so an old page gets 409 at once.
  • The root view and the Vite manifest are kept in memory.
  • A prop that can not become JSON gives an error that names the prop and its type.

Docs: Inertia

docs.title: OpenAPI
docs.text:
• paramResponses on RouteDoc: answers that only happen when the path has a param, like 404.
  • namedResponses: responses with a text key, like default or 2XX.
  • The body of a GET or DELETE route goes in the query string.

Docs: OpenAPI

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
• Package commands: a package adds its own dox commands with the dox: commands: key in its pubspec.yaml. dox help lists them. They work in a pub workspace too.
  • package:dox_core/command.dart with Command and MigrationFile, to write these commands.
  • dox migrate makes bin/migrate.dart when it is missing.
  • dox key:generate --show prints a new key and writes nothing.
  • --step given twice is an error.
  • dox serve --port=... prints a warning that says to set APP_PORT.

Docs: CLI, Package commands

docs.title: App template
docs.text:
The template that dox create uses got new files too.

  • Safer Docker Compose defaults, and a queue worker service.
  • AGENTS.md and the .agents/skills/dox skill: rules and recipes for AI coding tools. CLAUDE.md points to the same files (3.1.1).
  • Serializers live in lib/app/serializers/ (3.1.2).

docs.title: Redis client
docs.text:
• RedisOptions.fromUrl(url) reads a redis:// or rediss:// URL.
  • RedisSetOption is deprecated. It was empty and not used.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• back() only follows a Referer of the same host. Before, it was an open redirect.
  • ORM guarded could be skipped with a changed key, like ' is_admin' or 'IS_ADMIN'. Now the check trims the name and ignores case.
  • A local signed URL for one disk no longer works on the route of another disk.
  • Inertia ignores the Vite public/hot file when APP_ENV is production.
  • On MySQL, a key with a letter that is not ASCII can no longer set a guarded column.
  • Postgres: an unknown verify value now means the full certificate check.

docs.title: Routing and core
docs.text:
• A bad multipart body gets 400, not 500.
  • abort() headers are kept on routes with a next middleware.
  • A mounted handler that throws gives 500. Before, the client could hang.
  • A download name with quotes or non-ASCII letters gets a safe Content-Disposition.
  • res.withHeaders and res.header no longer drop or double headers.
  • A resumed download with If-Range no longer mixes two versions of a file. If-Range is used only when it matches the file's Last-Modified date or its strong ETag.
  • A Range header sent on two lines no longer gives 500.
  • req.session.reflash() keeps the flash data on the first use of the session.

docs.title: ORM and database
docs.text:
• A model write with no key and no where() no longer changes every row.
  • blog.update({...}) on a loaded model changes only that row and sets updated_at.
  • save() keeps an updated_at that you set.
  • A soft delete and restore() set updated_at too.
  • restore() on a query restores the soft deleted rows of the query.
  • reload() and preload clear a relation when the related rows are gone.
  • find('email', null) finds the row where email is null.
  • limit() with a negative number is ignored.
  • having('x', '!=', null) builds x IS NOT NULL.
  • update() and delete() with join(), orderBy() or limit() work on Postgres and SQLite.
  • foreignId('x').unique().constrained() compiles.
  • A failed nested transaction releases its savepoint.
  • @Unique and @Exists on Postgres with a value that does not fit the column no longer give 500.
  • @name inside a quoted string or a comment is no longer read as a param on MySQL and SQLite.
  • The query log lists the values in the right order.
  • Logger.warn prints yellow.
  • Rollback goes on when the file of a migration that already ran is gone.
  • MySQL 8.4 and Postgres: a text param is no longer stored with the wrong type after a table change.
  • MySQL 8.4: the same SQL with a number param first and a text param later no longer gives wrong rows.
  • Postgres: a broken server message gives an error, not a crash of the process.
  • Postgres: a query in a transaction is not sent again after a "cached plan" error.
  • MySQL: a slow DNS lookup when a pool opens no longer stops the other isolates.

docs.title: Auth
docs.text:
• The Bearer prefix is matched in any case.
  • A JWT check no longer hides unexpected errors. They go to the exception handler.
  • A request with two Authorization headers is a normal 401.

docs.title: Other packages
docs.text:
• Cache: FileDriver.prune() no longer deletes a value written at the same time.
  • Mail: Attachment.fromFile no longer blocks the server while it reads the file. An onError of FailoverTransport that throws no longer stops the failover.
  • Scheduler: schedule work ends a few seconds after Ctrl+C or SIGTERM. dailyAt('13') means 13:00. The overlap lock stays until the work really ends.
  • Socket.IO: CORS origin matching ignores case and a trailing /.
  • Views: {{ errors.email }} works with no session. A global named errors shows. The toJson() cache lasts one render.
  • Inertia: flash messages are kept after a deploy. A function prop inside a map or a list runs too.
  • CLI: migration:rollback --step 2 (with a space) works.
  • Redis client: the client waits for AUTH and SELECT before it sends commands. A failed AUTH on reconnect no longer crashes the app. The connect has a timeout. A server that closes the connection right after connect no longer crashes the app. The handshake tries again when the server is not ready yet (LOADING, BUSY, MASTERDOWN, TRYAGAIN). The wait between tries grows, and a long run of tries no longer ends in a stack overflow. disconnect() stops a try that is waiting.

docs.title: Full list
docs.text:
Every change is in the changelogs:

  • The Changelog page of the docs (dox_core, dox_builder, dox_annotation, dox_cache).
  • GitHub releases: dox, dox-orm, dox-auth, dox-validation, dox-mcp, dox-cli, dox-queue, dox-mailer, dox-scheduler, dox-storage, dox-socketio, dox-view, dox-inertia and dox-openapi.

docs.title: A tour of Dox features
docs.text:
This post is a short tour of the parts that come with Dox, from routing and validation to the ORM, login, queues, mail and the CLI.

Each item has one to three lines and a link to its docs page. Some parts are in the core package dox_core. Other parts are separate packages. You add only the ones you need.

docs.title: Core
docs.text:
• Routing: Routes for each HTTP method, route params, groups, resource routes and named routes. Signed routes and route model binding are included.
  • Middleware: Class or function middleware for one route, a group, a router or all routes. Request id, ETag and request timeout middleware come with it.
  • Request and response: Read input, headers, files and the client IP. Return a model, a map or a list, and Dox sends JSON. Files and big responses are streamed.
  • DTO validation: Write a @Dto class with rules on its fields. Dox checks the input and gives your controller a typed object. Bad input gets a 422 answer.
  • OpenAPI: dox_openapi makes OpenAPI 3.1 docs from your routes and DTOs. It also serves a docs page at /docs.
  • Sessions and CSRF: Sessions with a cookie or cache driver, and flash data. CSRF protection for forms.
  • Cookies: Set cookies on a response and read them from a request. Dox encrypts cookies with your APP_KEY.
  • Encryption and hashing: Crypt encrypts and decrypts text with the app key. Hash hashes and checks passwords. Hash.makeAsync and Hash.verifyAsync do not block the server.
  • Rate limiting: The RateLimit middleware stops a client that sends too many requests. With a Redis cache, all servers share the counts.
  • Security headers: The SecurityHeaders middleware sets safe default headers. You can change or turn off each header.
  • CORS: Allow one or more origins, and answer preflight requests.
  • Static files: Serve a folder or a storage disk with one line. You can also serve a single page app.
  • Health checks: A health route for a load balancer, Docker or Kubernetes. It can check the database and the cache.
  • IoC container: Add @Inject() to a class, and Dox makes it and its parameters for you. The container is generated code. It does not use reflection.
  • Providers: A provider sets up a package or a service when the app starts, and cleans up when it stops.
  • Exception handler: Every error goes to one handler. It logs the error and decides what the client gets.
  • Logging: The Logger prints colored text in development, or one JSON object per line for a log service.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
• ORM models: A model is a class for one table. Save, find, delete, hide fields and mass assignment rules are included.
  • Relations: Has one, has many, belongs to, many to many and polymorphic relations. You can query and count relations too.
  • Scopes and casts: A scope is a query part you use again and again. A cast changes a column value between the database and Dart, like JSON or an enum.
  • Factories and seeders: A factory makes models with sample data for tests. A seeder puts data in your database.
  • Migrations: Write the schema in Dart, then run, roll back or check migrations with the CLI.
  • Query builder and transactions: Build SQL from chained methods with bound values. Run many queries in one transaction.
  • Databases: Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite. Postgres and MySQL use native drivers.

docs.title: Auth
docs.text:
• Guards: Use more than one guard in one app, or write your own, like an API key guard.
  • JWT: dox_auth logs users in with JWT tokens. Tokens can be revoked.
  • Session login: Log users in with a session cookie for web pages.
  • Access tokens: Tokens saved in the database, with abilities. You can revoke them one by one.
  • Gates and policies: A gate checks one action. A policy groups the checks for one model. Use them in a controller or on a route.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
• Cache: dox_cache comes with dox_core, so there is nothing to add. It has memory, file and Redis stores, with tags and locks.
  • Queue: dox_queue runs slow work in the background. It has Redis, database and sync drivers, retries, delays and a worker.
  • Scheduler: dox_scheduler runs tasks on a schedule, like cron. You write the schedule in Dart.
  • Mail and notifications: dox_mailer sends email with SMTP, Amazon SES, Resend, Mailgun, Postmark and more. A notification can go out on more than one channel.
  • Storage: dox_storage gives one API for local disk, AWS S3 and S3-compatible services, with signed URLs.
  • Socket.IO: dox_socketio is a Socket.IO v4 server. The official clients connect with no changes.
  • Views: dox_view is an HTML template engine. Templates are .dox.html files.
  • Inertia: dox_inertia lets you build a single page app with React, Vue or Svelte, with routes and controllers in Dox.
  • MCP: dox_mcp serves tools to MCP clients from a normal Dox route. Tool arguments are checked before your code runs.
  • Redis: Redis is not a separate package to install. It is a driver in the cache, the queue and the Socket.IO adapter. These packages bring their own Redis client. Use Redis when you run more than one server.

docs.title: Tooling
docs.text:
• CLI generators: dox make:controller, make:model, make:dto, make:middleware, make:migration, make:factory, make:seeder, make:job and more.
  • Testing helpers: DoxTestClient runs the app inside a test. It can keep a session and log in as a user.
  • dox build: Builds the app into one native binary. It does not need the Dart SDK.
  • Docker: The project has a Dockerfile and a compose file. The image holds only the binary and the files it needs.
  • App template: dox create starts from this template. It has an AGENTS.md file and a skill with step-by-step recipes for AI coding tools.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text: Install the CLI and make your first project: Installation.

docs.title: Dox vs Go: speed and memory
docs.text: In our published benchmark on 2 CPU cores, a Dox app handled 2× to 4.8× the requests per second of a Go app. Go used less memory once a database was added.

docs.title: The short answer
docs.text:
Requests per second at 256 connections. The last column shows how many times the requests of Go that Dox handled:

Test Dox Go Dox handles Plain HTTP, GET / 638,067 242,043 2.6× Plain HTTP, GET /user/:id 572,658 230,845 2.5× Plain HTTP, POST /user 545,986 231,050 2.4× JSON, GET /json 555,216 206,398 2.7× One row from Postgres, GET /db 266,432 55,903 4.8× 20 rows from Postgres, GET /queries?n=20 17,772 6,635 2.7× One row from MySQL, GET /db 247,242 55,322 4.5× 20 rows from MySQL, GET /queries?n=20 12,347 5,520 2.2×

The smallest gap is 2×, on GET / at 64 connections. The JSON row is from the Postgres run.

This post compares Dox with Go only. The full tables also have other servers. You can find them, and the full method, on the Performance page. Every number here comes from that page.

docs.title: How it was measured
docs.text:
• Docker on an Apple M2, with 8 CPUs in the Docker VM (linux/arm64).
  • The server gets 2 CPUs. The load tool (wrk 4.1) runs on other CPUs.
  • One server runs at a time. Connections use keep-alive.
  • Each server has one worker per core. Dox has one isolate per core. Go is one process with GOMAXPROCS=2.
  • Dox is an AOT build (dox build) with Dart 3.13.6. Go is version 1.26.
  • The Go app uses the standard library server, net/http. We did not test other Go servers or frameworks.
  • 5 seconds of warm-up, then 15 seconds per route.
  • Peak memory is the peak of the whole container.

docs.title: Plain HTTP
docs.text:
The test follows the rules of the-benchmarker/web-frameworks. Dox is a full Dox app with three routes. Go uses net/http with http.ServeMux.

Requests per second on 2 cores

GET /, 256 connections. Higher is better.

req/s Doxfull app 638,067fastest Gonet/http 242,0432.6× slower

Dox · Go 1.26 · Dart 3.13 · 2 cores · 256 connections · wrk

Peak memory on 2 cores

GET /, 256 connections. Peak memory of the container, lower is better.

peak Doxfull app 19 MBlowest Gonet/http 36 MB1.9× more

Dox · Go 1.26 · Dart 3.13 · 2 cores · 256 connections · wrk

GET /, requests per second:

Server 64 connections 256 connections 512 connections p99 at 256 peak MB Dox 494,223 638,067 612,032 0.74 ms 19 Go (net/http) 248,951 242,043 232,687 3.27 ms 36

The other two routes, at 256 connections:

Server GET /user/:id POST /user Dox 572,658 545,986 Go 230,845 231,050

Dox handled 2× the requests of Go at 64 connections, and 2.6× at 256 and 512 connections. On the other two routes it handled 2.5× and 2.4×. Its peak memory was 19 MB. Go's peak was 36 MB. Both are small.

docs.title: A small app with a database
docs.text:
This test is closer to a real app:

  • GET /json returns a map as JSON.
  • GET /db reads one row by id.
  • GET /queries?n=20 reads 20 rows, one after another.

Each app uses its database driver directly, with no ORM. Dox uses dox_postgres_native or dox_mysql_native. Go uses pgx or go-sql-driver. The server gets 2 CPUs and the database gets 2 CPUs. Each server has 8 database connections in total. There was one run of 15 seconds per route.

Read one row on 2 cores

GET /db on Postgres 18, 256 connections. Higher is better.

req/s Doxdox_postgres_native 266,432fastest Gopgx 55,9034.8× slower

Dox · Go 1.26 · Dart 3.13 · Postgres 18 · 2 cores · 256 connections · wrk

Peak memory with Postgres on 2 cores

256 connections. Peak memory of the container, lower is better.

peak Gopgx 31 MBlowest Doxdox_postgres_native 106 MB3.4× more

Dox · Go 1.26 · Dart 3.13 · Postgres 18 · 2 cores · 256 connections · wrk

Postgres 18, requests per second at 256 connections:

Server /json /db /queries?n=20 peak MB Dox (dox_postgres_native) 555,216 266,432 17,772 106 Go (net/http + pgx) 206,398 55,903 6,635 31

MySQL 8.4, requests per second at 256 connections:

Server /json /db /queries?n=20 peak MB Dox (dox_mysql_native) 558,886 247,242 12,347 70 Go (net/http + go-sql-driver) 211,713 55,322 5,520 27

On /db with Postgres, the p99 was 1.8 ms for Dox and 6.3 ms for Go.

Three things to see here:

  • Dox handled more requests on every route. The gap is largest on /db: 4.8× with Postgres and 4.5× with MySQL.
  • On /json it handled 2.7×. On 20 queries per request it handled 2.7× with Postgres and 2.2× with MySQL.
  • Go used less memory. Its peak was 31 MB with Postgres and 27 MB with MySQL. The peak of Dox was 106 MB and 70 MB.

docs.title: Why the numbers differ
docs.text:
We did not profile the Go app. So we can not say where its time goes. But the two servers are built in different ways:

  • How a request runs. In Dox, the native HTTP server runs on the thread of the isolate. One call writes the answers, reads the sockets and parses the new requests. Under load, no other thread is involved. In Go, net/http starts one goroutine per connection, and the Go scheduler runs the goroutines on the threads.
  • How a query is sent. The Dox drivers send many queries down one connection at once (pipelining). In the Go app, each query takes one connection from the pool and waits for its answer. With 8 connections, at most 8 queries run at the same time.
  • Memory. Both are one process with a compiled binary and no JIT compiler. This helps both stay small on plain HTTP. We did not measure why Dox needs more memory than Go when a database is added.

What makes Dox fast explains the Dox side in more detail.

docs.title: Measure your own app
docs.text:
These numbers come from one machine and very small apps. Your app is different. It has more routes, more data and its own code. A real app spends most of its time on the database, JSON and your own logic. So the gap in your app can be smaller or larger.

Before you choose, build your app with dox build and measure it on your own server. The Performance page shows how we ran the tests, so you can run them the same way.

docs.title: Dox vs Node.js: memory and speed
docs.text:
In our published benchmark on 2 CPU cores, a Dox app served more requests per second than a Node.js app and used much less memory.

This post compares Dox with Node.js only. The full tables also have other servers. You can find them, and the full method, on the Performance page. Every number here comes from that page.

docs.title: How it was measured
docs.text:
• Docker on an Apple M2, with 8 CPUs in the Docker VM (linux/arm64).
  • The server gets 2 CPUs. The load tool (wrk 4.1) runs on other CPUs.
  • One server runs at a time. Connections use keep-alive.
  • Each server has one worker per core. Dox has one isolate per core. Node has one process per core (node:cluster).
  • Dox is an AOT build (dox build) with Dart 3.13.6. Node is version 26.12.
  • 5 seconds of warm-up, then 15 seconds per route.
  • Peak memory is the peak of the whole container. It counts every process in the container. For Node, that includes the cluster primary process, which does not serve requests.

docs.title: Plain HTTP
docs.text:
The test follows the rules of the-benchmarker/web-frameworks. Dox is a full Dox app with three routes. Node uses node:http.

Requests per second on 2 cores

GET /, 256 connections. Higher is better.

req/s Doxfull app 638,067fastest Nodenode:http 286,8472.2× slower

Dox · Node 26 · Dart 3.13 · 2 cores · 256 connections · wrk

Peak memory on 2 cores

GET /, 256 connections. Peak memory of the container, lower is better.

peak Doxfull app 19 MBlowest Nodenode:http 200 MB10.5× more

Dox · Node 26 · Dart 3.13 · 2 cores · 256 connections · wrk

GET /, requests per second:

Server 64 connections 256 connections 512 connections p99 at 256 peak MB Dox 494,223 638,067 612,032 0.74 ms 19 Node (node:http) 252,866 286,847 296,257 1.70 ms 200

The other two routes, at 256 connections:

Server GET /user/:id POST /user Dox 572,658 545,986 Node 274,067 301,084

At 256 connections, Dox served about 2.2 times more requests than Node on GET /. Its peak memory was 19 MB. Node's peak was 200 MB.

docs.title: A small app with a database
docs.text:
This test is closer to a real app:

  • GET /json returns a map as JSON.
  • GET /db reads one row by id.
  • GET /queries?n=20 reads 20 rows, one after another.

Each app uses its database driver directly, with no ORM. Dox uses dox_postgres_native or dox_mysql_native. Node uses pg or mysql2. The server gets 2 CPUs and the database gets 2 CPUs. Each server has 4 database connections per core, so 8 in total. There was one run of 15 seconds per route.

Read one row on 2 cores

GET /db on Postgres 18, 256 connections. Higher is better.

req/s Doxdox_postgres_native 266,432fastest Nodepg 75,4473.5× slower

Dox · Node 26 · Dart 3.13 · Postgres 18 · 2 cores · 256 connections · wrk

Postgres 18, requests per second at 256 connections:

Server /json /db /queries?n=20 peak MB Dox (dox_postgres_native) 555,216 266,432 17,772 106 Node (node:http + pg) 205,774 75,447 7,458 232

MySQL 8.4, requests per second at 256 connections:

Server /json /db /queries?n=20 peak MB Dox (dox_mysql_native) 558,886 247,242 12,347 70 Node (node:http + mysql2) 205,630 74,809 6,001 239

On /db with Postgres, the p99 was 1.8 ms for Dox and 4.1 ms for Node.

Two things to see here:

  • Dox uses more memory with a database than without one: 106 MB with Postgres and 70 MB with MySQL, against 19 MB for plain HTTP.
  • Node also uses more memory, and stays at or above 200 MB in all three tests.

docs.title: Why Dox uses less memory
docs.text:
We did not measure where each megabyte goes. But these design choices make a difference:

  • One process. Dox runs one process with one isolate per core. The isolates share one compiled program. The Node app runs one process per core plus a primary process, and each one loads its own JavaScript engine and its own copy of the app.
  • No JIT compiler. dox build makes an AOT binary, so no compiler runs next to your app. Node compiles JavaScript while the app runs.
  • Socket work outside the Dart heap. The native HTTP server reads the sockets and parses HTTP in native code.
  • One database pool. All isolates share one pool for the whole process.

What makes Dox fast explains each of these in more detail.

docs.title: Measure your own app
docs.text:
These numbers come from one machine and very small apps. Your app is different. It has more routes, more data and its own code. A real app spends most of its time on the database, JSON and your own logic. So the gap in your app can be smaller or larger.

Before you choose, build your app with dox build and measure it on your own server. The Performance page shows how we ran the tests, so you can run them the same way.

docs.title: Live updates with Socket.IO in Dox
docs.text:
This post shows how to add live updates to a Dox app with Socket.IO. When one user changes data, the screens of the other users change too, with no refresh.

The example is a team app. Many people work in one project. When one member adds a task, the other members should see it at once, with no refresh.

dox_socketio is a Socket.IO v4 server. The official socket.io-client connects to it with no changes. It runs on the same port as your HTTP routes, at /socket.io/.

docs.title: The steps in short
docs.text:
It is four small files on the server and one on the client:

  1. dart pub add dox_socketio
  2. lib/providers/socket_io_provider.dart: starts Socket.IO. Three lines.
  3. lib/config/socketio.dart: websocket only, your own sites only.
  4. lib/app/socket/live.namespace.dart: signs in the user and joins their room.
  5. lib/app/services/live.service.dart: sends a changed event after a write.
  6. src/lib/live.ts: the client connects and loads the data again on each event.

Many isolates work with no extra setup and no Redis. The rest of this post goes through each step.

docs.title: The plan
docs.text:
• Each user signs in to the socket with the same token the app already uses for the API.
  • Each socket joins a room for its user: user:<id>.
  • After a write, the server sends a small changed event to the users who can see that data.
  • The event holds only a topic, like tasks. It never holds the data.
  • The app gets the event and loads that data again through the normal API.

Why no data in the event? The API already checks who may see what. If the event only says "tasks changed", those checks stay in one place. A bug in the socket code can not leak data.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
dart pub add dox_socketio

npm install socket.io-client

docs.title: 2. The provider
docs.text:
The provider starts Socket.IO in every isolate. Make the file lib/providers/socket_io_provider.dart. It must be in lib/providers/, so the generated container finds it:

lib/providers/socket_io_provider.dart
import 'package:dox_socketio/dox_socketio.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/socketio.dart';

class AppSocketIoProvider extends SocketIoProvider {
  AppSocketIoProvider() : super(socketIoConfig);
}

docs.title: 3. The config
docs.text:
Make the file lib/config/socketio.dart:

lib/config/socketio.dart
import 'package:dox_socketio/dox_socketio.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/socket/live.namespace.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/settings.dart';

SocketIoConfig socketIoConfig = SocketIoConfig(
  options: ServerOptions(
    transports: const <String>['websocket'],
    allowedOrigins: <String>[settings.appUrl, ...settings.frontendUrls],
  ),
  namespaces: <NamespaceHandler>[LiveNamespace()],
);

Two settings matter here:

  • transports: ['websocket']. Dox runs one isolate per CPU core. One websocket stays on one isolate. Long-polling sends many HTTP requests, and they can reach different isolates. So allow websocket only.
  • allowedOrigins. Only your own pages may open a socket. Other websites get 403.

docs.title: 4. Sign in the socket
docs.text:
Socket.IO gets its requests before the router, so your route auth middleware does not run. Use SocketAuth as a namespace middleware instead. Your function gets the handshake and returns the user, or null.

Make the file lib/app/socket/live.namespace.dart:

lib/app/socket/live.namespace.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_socketio/dox_socketio.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/services/live.service.dart';

class LiveNamespace extends NamespaceHandler {
  @override
  String get path => '/';

  @override
  List<Middleware> get middleware => <Middleware>[SocketAuth(findUser).handle];

  /// The same checks as the API auth middleware.
  static Future<User?> findUser(Handshake handshake) async {
    String? token = handshake.token;
    if (token == null || token.isEmpty) return null;
    return Dox().ioc.get<UserService>().findByToken(token);
  }

  @override
  void onConnection(Socket socket) {
    User user = socket.user! as User;
    socket.join(LiveService.roomOf(user.id!));
  }
}
  • handshake.token is auth.token from the client.
  • With null, the client gets a connect_error with Unauthorized, and onConnection does not run.
  • The token is checked once, when the socket connects.

findUser can check any token your API already uses. With dox_auth, use Auth(guard: 'api').userFromToken(token). See Log in a socket.

docs.title: 5. Send events after a write
docs.text:
A small service sends the events. SocketIoProvider.server is the Socket.IO server of this isolate.

Make the file lib/app/services/live.service.dart:

lib/app/services/live.service.dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_socketio/dox_socketio.dart';

@Inject()
class LiveService {
  LiveService(this.projectMembers);

  final ProjectMemberRepository projectMembers;

  static String roomOf(int userId) => 'user:$userId';

  /// Data of [projectId] changed: tell its members.
  Future<void> projectChanged(int projectId, String topic) async {
    try {
      Set<int> users = await projectMembers.userIdsOf(projectId);
      await _emit(users, <String, Object>{'topic': topic, 'projectId': projectId});
    } catch (error) {
      Logger.warn('[live] project $projectId $topic: $error');
    }
  }

  /// Something everyone sees changed, like a notice for all users.
  Future<void> everyoneChanged(String topic) async {
    await SocketIoProvider.server?.emit('changed', <String, Object>{'topic': topic});
  }

  Future<void> _emit(Set<int> users, Map<String, Object> data) async {
    SocketIoServer? io = SocketIoProvider.server;
    if (io == null || users.isEmpty) return;
    BroadcastOperator to = io.to(roomOf(users.first));
    for (int user in users.skip(1)) {
      to = to.to(roomOf(user));
    }
    await to.emit('changed', data);
  }
}

Then call it from your services, after the write. For example, in lib/app/services/task.service.dart:

lib/app/services/task.service.dart
Future<Task> create(int projectId, Map<String, dynamic> data) async {
  Task task = await tasks.create(projectId, data);
  await live.projectChanged(projectId, 'tasks');
  return task;
}
  • A failed send is logged. It never fails the write.
  • to(a).to(b) sends one event to many rooms. A user in two rooms gets it once.
  • Put the calls in services, not controllers. Then queue jobs, scheduled jobs and other entry points send events too.

docs.title: 6. Many isolates, no Redis
docs.text:
Each isolate has its own Socket.IO server, and a client is connected to one of them. So an event sent from isolate 1 must also reach clients on isolate 3.

You do not need to do anything for this. With many isolates, the provider uses the IsolateAdapter. It sends each broadcast to the other isolates of the process. You need no Redis.

With more than one server process, use the Redis adapter.

docs.title: 7. The client
docs.text:
In the frontend, make the file src/lib/live.ts:

src/lib/live.ts
import { io, type Socket } from 'socket.io-client'

let socket: Socket | null = null
let connectedOnce = false

/** Call after sign-in. */
export function startLive() {
  if (socket) return
  socket = io(window.location.origin, {
    transports: ['websocket'],
    auth: sendToken,
  })
  socket.on('connect', onConnect)
  socket.on('changed', onChanged)
}

/** Call on sign-out. */
export function stopLive() {
  socket?.disconnect()
  socket = null
  connectedOnce = false
}

/** A fresh token on every connect and reconnect. */
async function sendToken(done: (data: object) => void) {
  done({ token: (await getToken()) ?? '' })
}

/** Events sent while we were offline are lost, so a reconnect loads all. */
function onConnect() {
  if (connectedOnce) reloadAll()
  connectedOnce = true
}

function onChanged(change: { topic: string; projectId?: number }) {
  if (change.topic === 'tasks' && change.projectId === activeProjectId()) {
    reloadTasks()
  }
  // ... one line per topic
}

Three things to note:

  • auth is a function, not an object. The client calls it on each reconnect, so a token that expired is replaced.
  • Socket.IO does not keep events for a client that is offline. On reconnect, load everything again.
  • transports: ['websocket'] must match the server.

docs.title: 8. The dev proxy
docs.text:
If your frontend dev server proxies the API, add /socket.io with websocket support. With Vite, add it to vite.config.ts:

vite.config.ts
server: {
  proxy: {
    '/api': 'http://localhost:3000',
    '/socket.io': { target: 'http://localhost:3000', ws: true },
  },
},

Without ws: true, the socket can not connect in dev.

docs.title: 9. Test it
docs.text:
You can test it with the real client, from Dart, with the socket_io_client package. A good set of tests:

  • A bad token is refused.
  • A new task reaches the project members, and not a user outside the project.
  • A user who is not signed in gets no events.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• Live screens for every user, with no refresh.
  • No data in the events, so the API access checks stay in one place.
  • It works on every isolate, with no Redis.
  • The standard socket.io-client works with no changes.

Full docs: Socket.IO

docs.title: What makes Dox fast
docs.text:
Dox is fast because your Dart code runs as a compiled binary, the network and database work happens in native code on the same thread, and most of the setup work is done once at build time or at start.

Your app is plain Dart: routes, controllers, DTOs, middleware and models. This post explains what Dox does around that code, one reason at a time. Each section links to the docs page with the details.

docs.title: A compiled binary
docs.text:
dox build compiles your app ahead of time (AOT) into a native binary. The code is machine code before the server starts. No compiler runs next to your app, and the server needs no Dart SDK.

dart run and dox serve use the JIT compiler. They are for development. They use much more memory and start slower. Always run the AOT binary in production.

See Deployment.

docs.title: A native HTTP server on the isolate's thread
docs.text:
Every Dox app runs on dox_http_native. It is written in Rust. It owns the sockets and parses HTTP. Your code still runs in Dart.

The server works in a loop on the isolate's own thread:

  1. Dart makes one call into the native code.
  2. The native code writes the answers of the last batch, reads the sockets and parses the new requests. It gives them to Dart as one batch.
  3. Dart runs your handlers and makes the next call with their answers.

Under load, no other thread is involved. So a request never waits for another thread to wake up. A small helper thread only watches the sockets while the isolate is idle.

The server has the same API as the dart:io HttpServer. Code written for dart:io keeps working.

See Native server.

docs.title: One isolate per CPU core
docs.text:
Dox starts one isolate per CPU core by default. Each isolate runs the whole app and its own server on the same port. The operating system spreads the connections between them.

All isolates live in one process and share the compiled program. You do not need a process manager to use all cores.

See Isolate.

docs.title: Keep-alive and pipelining
docs.text:
A connection stays open for the next request (keep-alive). A client can also send many requests on one connection without waiting for each answer (pipelining).

There are limits, so one client can not fill the memory. At most 64 requests of one connection wait for an answer. At most 1 MB of answers waits to be sent. Then the server stops reading that connection until the answers go out.

See Native server: limits.

docs.title: Native database drivers
docs.text:
Postgres and MySQL use native drivers: dox_postgres_native and dox_mysql_native. Your models and queries stay in Dart. You do not change any config.

  • The database work runs on the thread of each isolate, like the HTTP server. There is no extra thread to hand a query to.
  • Many queries go down one connection at once (pipelining).
  • Dart sends many queries in one call. The results come back together.
  • All isolates share one pool. The pool size is for the whole process, so the database gets a known number of connections.

See Native Postgres driver, Native MySQL driver and the package READMEs on GitHub: dox-postgres-native and dox-mysql-native.

docs.title: Generated code, not reflection
docs.text:
Dox does not use dart:mirrors. Instead, build_runner with dox_builder writes plain Dart code for you:

  • the dependency injection container (lib/generated/container.g.dart),
  • the list of your Router classes, in the same file,
  • the DTO checks (a .dto.g.dart file next to each DTO),
  • the model classes.

The DTO rules, like @Email() or @Min(18), become typed Dart code at build time. They are not rule strings that are read on each request. This is also what makes the AOT build possible.

See Dependency injection and Validation.

docs.title: Work done once, not on each request
docs.text:
When an isolate starts, it does some work once:

  • It builds the pattern of each route.
  • It reads the parameter types of each controller.
  • It groups the routes by HTTP method.

On each request, Dox does less:

  • JSON and text responses are encoded once, straight to bytes, with Content-Length set.
  • LogMiddleware collects log lines and writes them in one write every 20 ms (or every 64 KB). In a new project it is off in production.

See Performance: what Dox does for you and How Dox works.

docs.title: What Dox does not do
docs.text:
Some choices are left to you on purpose:

  • No VM flags. Dox never sets Dart VM flags for you. We tried a bigger young generation for a better p99. The change was inside the noise, so there is no flag to set. You can try your own with DART_VM_OPTIONS.
  • No gzip in Dart by default. gzip costs CPU on every response. A proxy like Caddy or nginx does it better. If you have no proxy, AppConfig(compress: true) turns it on, and the native server gzips on a helper thread.

See Performance: Dart VM flags and Performance: gzip.

docs.title: A few numbers
docs.text:
On 2 CPU cores, GET / with 256 connections, a full Dox app served 638,067 requests per second. A plain dart:io HttpServer, with no framework, served 129,796. In a small app that reads one row from Postgres (GET /db), Dox served 266,432 requests per second.

These numbers come from one machine and very small apps. A real app spends most of its time on the database, JSON and your own code, so the gaps are smaller there. Measure your own app. The Performance page has the full tables and how they were measured.
